To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have used a new computational method to identify genes that are highly reproducible in their expression pattern across the human brain and that these genes are enriched for brain-related annotations and are involved in many neurodevelopmental and neurological disorders.
We developed a novel method for identifying reproducible gene expression patterns across the adult human brain.

(1) we have identified highly reproducible gene expression patterning in the adult human brain; (2) we have developed a method to quantify this reproducibility; and (3) we have used this metric to identify 32 gene expression signatures, including those that are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and interpretation of the most reproducible patterns of gene expression in the human brain.
the identification of the genetic architecture that is common to all adult human brains and the identification of the most stable genes and gene expression signatures across the adult human brain.
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying human brain development, and how these relate to the function of the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have identified the most robust gene expression signatures in human brain and their relevance to human brain function and dysfunction.
the genes with the highest stability across the brain are enriched for genes that are highly biologically and clinically relevant.

this work has provided a comprehensive analysis of the genetic signatures of the human brain and their relationship with neuroanatomy, disease and function, and has provided a foundation for future studies of human neurodevelopment and neurological disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified 32 canonical genetic signatures of the human brain that represent distinct cell types and/or intracellular components and associations with neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration.

we have identified a large collection of genes that are consistently expressed in the human brain across individuals and across brain regions, which we call the canonical genetic signature of the brain.
the adult human brain has a highly reproducible and consistent transcriptional architecture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified a set of 32 genes that are highly stable in the brain across individuals.
the human brain exhibits highly conserved gene expression patterning, which may be important for its stereotyped development and function.

there is a highly reproducible genetic architecture of the adult brain, which is associated with functionally relevant circuit connectivity and which is enriched for genes with brain-related annotations.
